title: Asia 6 of 7 · East Asia
edition: Asia countries · Seven regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Asia episode six of seven. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.

Six map targets form our East Asian route: China, Mongolia, Taiwan, North Korea, South Korea and Japan. Taiwan’s separate target is a geographic teaching choice, not a settlement of its political status.

states.name: China
lines: China is the broad eastern mainland country south of Mongolia and Russia. The Korean Peninsula and Japan lie beyond its eastern side; India and the Himalayan countries are to the southwest.
The Great Wall was developed across many periods, joining and extending older defences. It is a network with a long history, rather than one wall built in a single project.
Picture a long defensive frontier across northern China, below Mongolia. Use the broad mainland outline first, then place the smaller eastern neighbours around it.
states.transition: Let's bring China and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Mongolia
lines: Mongolia is the large landlocked country between Russia and China. It has no direct border with Kazakhstan, despite coming close to its eastern end.
The Orkhon Valley contains the remains of Karakorum, a capital of the Mongol Empire. Pastureland and traces of imperial government sit together in the same cultural landscape.
Remember a steppe country sandwiched between two giants, Russia above and China below. Picture an imperial capital amid grazing lands, rather than looking for a coast.
states.transition: Let's bring Mongolia and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Taiwan
lines: Taiwan is the island off China’s southeastern coast, north of the Philippines and southwest of Japan’s main islands. The Taiwan Strait separates it from the mainland.
Taipei’s National Palace Museum holds a jadeite cabbage with tiny carved insects. The artist used the stone’s natural green and white colours to imitate leaves and stalk.

Picture the jade cabbage on the island across the strait. Taiwan is self-governed and claimed by China; we follow its separate GeoClick target without treating the map as a settlement of political status.
states.transition: Let's bring Taiwan and its neighbours into view.

states.name: North Korea
lines: North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula, below China and above South Korea. A short northeastern border touches Russia.
Ancient Koguryo tombs preserve painted scenes of daily life and beliefs. Their history reaches back many centuries before the modern division of Korea.
Remember painted tombs in the northern half of the peninsula. The two Korean map targets are neighbours on the same peninsula; Japan is across the sea to the east.
states.transition: Let's bring North Korea and its neighbours into view.

states.name: South Korea
lines: South Korea occupies the southern part of the Korean Peninsula, below North Korea. Its shores face seas on three sides, with Japan across the water to the east.
Haeinsa Temple safeguards Buddhist texts carved on around eighty thousand wooden printing blocks. Their purpose-built storage buildings helped preserve this enormous wooden library.
Picture a library made of carved wood in the peninsula’s southern half. North Korea above, South Korea below: the paired location comes before the extra fact.

states.name: Japan
lines: Japan is the island arc east of Korea and the Asian mainland. Its main islands run roughly northeast to southwest, with Hokkaido toward the north and Kyushu toward the south.
Yakushima, south of Kyushu, preserves ancient Japanese cedar trees. This forested island is a reminder that Japan includes exceptional natural landscapes as well as densely built cities.
Picture old cedar trees on the island arc beyond Korea. Keep Japan offshore, and remember that the main islands are only part of a much wider island country.
states.transition: Let's bring Japan and its neighbours into view.

recap: China is the broad mainland, Mongolia the landlocked country above it. Taiwan lies off the southeastern coast; North and South Korea share a peninsula, and Japan forms the island arc beyond them.

Recall the long-built wall, steppe capital, jade cabbage, painted tombs, wooden printing library and ancient cedar forest. Asian Russia continues north of this group; we orient it here without repeating the Europe lesson.
